Six static dashboards built from the unified warehouse marts, ordered by
the decision each one informs rather than by the order they were built.
Every panel is tagged with the audit question it answers; the full
question-by-question checklist (nine questions, each unanswerable or wrong
from any single silo) lives in the
[silo audit memo](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/docs/silo_audit.md).
The models that turn three of these findings into recommendations are on the
[models and experiments](models.qmd) page; the recommendations themselves
are in the [strategy memo](strategy-memo.qmd).

Every frame below is the real artifact, embedded as-is; the source build is
[analysis/dashboards](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/tree/main/analysis/dashboards),
and every derived figure quoted here is recomputed by
[derived_figures.py](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/analysis/dashboards/derived_figures.py).

## 1. Consumer identity and what duplicates cost

**Decision this informs:** whether the marketplace should suppress or
re-price recently sold consumers itself, rather than leave it to buyers.

2.40M auction lead ids and 2.28M CRM lead ids resolve to 635,579
consumers; 69% of applications are repeats; the 20% of consumers with five
or more applications produce 53% of revenue; 112,049 orphaned applications
are restored from the lake. Buyers paid **$12.0M (5.7% of revenue)** for
consumers they had already bought within 30 days, and $48.3M (23.1%) of
revenue is re-sales of a consumer any buyer had bought within 30 days --
the leakage that remains after buyers' own suppression and discounting,
with the window's sensitivity charted from 1 to 90 days.

<iframe class="dashboard-frame" data-src="embedded/04_consumer_identity.html" title="Consumer identity dashboard" loading="lazy"></iframe>

[Open full page](embedded/04_consumer_identity.html){target="_blank"}

::: {.callout-note title="Why the duplicate-spend figure is $12.0M and not $40.0M"}
The first version of these dashboards reported $40.0M (14% of revenue) paid by buyers for consumers they had bought within the prior 30 days, and a funded rate that was flat across tiers and prices. The human flagged both as "troublesome" and supplied a duplicate-performance table from industry experience: consumers who return soon after a prior lead win less and clear lower (prompt P-011). The engine learned buyer-side recency suppression and a modest price gradient on funding (decision C19), was redeployed end to end, and overall sell-through moved from the invented ~60% to the source data's 49%. The residual leakage after that suppression is the $12.0M (5.7%) shown here; the earlier figure stands in the record as history, not as an error.
:::

## 2. Marketing attribution: which channels earn their spend

**Decision this informs:** where the next acquisition dollar goes, and
whether display spend continues.

$194.3M of $209.2M revenue (93%) is attributable to a marketing contact and
$104.5M to paid channels, on $53.8M of paid spend (blended ROAS 1.94x).
Channel ROAS runs from 0.94x (display, below break-even: $11.6M spent for
$10.9M of revenue) to 3.06x (affiliate); cost per sold lead runs from $57
(affiliate) to $183 (display). The click ranking the marketing silo can
compute alone inverts this ordering. Cohort ROAS is right-censored for
recent months, so the chart compares channels within a month; a
maturity-adjusted projection is the open analysis item.

## 3. The nurture experiment and who to message

**Decision this informs:** whom the nurture program should message at all,
and whether the experiment can support a level claim.

Read honestly: +0.109pp application lift against an injected +0.115pp, with
a 95% interval of -0.105 to +0.324pp -- the experiment is underpowered for
the pooled effect at this scale (it would need about 6.1M contacts against
859k available), and the dashboard says so rather than torturing
significance out of it. What it can support is a ranking: the injected
effect is concentrated in one engagement segment, the naive read and the
uplift model both recover that concentration, and the resulting send policy
is on the [models page](models.qmd) with the power arithmetic in the
[experiment read-out](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/docs/experiment_readout.md).

## 4. Auction economics: where the revenue is

**Decision this informs:** where reserve floors should sit, and which
segments the schedule should be shaped around.

Tier 1 carries 83% of revenue, sells 28.4% of the leads offered to it at a
mean $255 against a $187 floor, and its median clearing price equals the
floor in every FICO band -- more than half of tier-1 sales are floor-pinned,
so the floor is the price for most of the revenue base. Earnings per lead
offered in tier 1 run from $51 (FICO 600-659) to $81 (780+); recent repeat
applicants clear at 0.52-0.75x fresh prices. Buyer concentration (HHI about
3,120 in every tier) is a construction of the five-buyer panels in the
auction landscape, and the dashboard says so.

## 5. The full funnel

**Decision this informs:** whether higher-priced leads are also better
leads for buyers -- the quality argument behind a stiffer tier-1 floor.

Message to application to auction to sale to funded loan in one view: stage
volumes, stage-to-stage conversion by acquisition channel, and funded rate by
tier and clearing-price band. 12.7% of sold leads fund^[Three funded-rate
denominators appear across the project, all correct: 12.7% counts every sold
lead; 13.3% excludes the 55,328 sold migration orphans whose CRM outcome is
lost; 13.4% is the CRM's own funded-on-sold rate before unification. The
dashboards state which one each panel uses.], declining from 14.3% in tier 1
to 8.5% in tier 6 and rising with price from 8.4% (under $10) to 15.7%
($300+). The gradient is a calibrated direction in the simulated world, so
it supports the argument only as far as the calibration does.

## 6. Before and after: what a single silo would have told you

**Decision this informs:** none directly -- this is the evidence that the
five findings above could not have been produced from any one system, and
the scorecard for the nine audit questions.

What each silo believed alone versus what the unified view shows: headcount
by system versus resolved consumers, and paid-channel ROI where the
click-value ranking inverts once revenue is joined through the auction.

```{=html}
<script>
// Load each dashboard iframe only as it approaches the viewport. Six eager
// frames each pull their own copy of plotly.js; deferring to scroll keeps
// initial load light while the "Open full page" links remain the no-JS path.
(function () {
  var frames = document.querySelectorAll("iframe[data-src]");
  if (!("IntersectionObserver" in window)) {
    frames.forEach(function (f) { f.src = f.dataset.src; });
    return;
  }
  var io = new IntersectionObserver(function (entries) {
    entries.forEach(function (e) {
      if (e.isIntersecting) {
        e.target.src = e.target.dataset.src;
        io.unobserve(e.target);
      }
    });
  }, { rootMargin: "200px" });
  // Arm on first interaction: nothing heavy loads until the visitor starts
  // reading (any scroll, tap, or keypress), then frames stream in as they
  // approach the viewport.
  var armed = false;
  function arm() {
    if (armed) return;
    armed = true;
    frames.forEach(function (f) { io.observe(f); });
  }
  ["scroll", "pointerdown", "keydown", "touchstart"].forEach(function (ev) {
    window.addEventListener(ev, arm, { once: true, passive: true });
  });
})();
</script>
```
